Data Lunch is a short course in applied statistics. It starts from a single uncomfortable
claim, that most published research findings are false, and rebuilds statistics so you
can tell when a finding deserves to be believed.

The course is Bayesian, in the style of McElreath's *Statistical Rethinking*. We think
about causes before we touch the data, draw our assumptions as causal diagrams (DAGs),
write models in [Stan](https://mc-stan.org), and check every model on simulated data
before trusting it on real data. Students apply each week's ideas to their own question
using World Bank development indicators.

# Lectures

Each week is a slide deck. Most weeks have a concepts part and an applied part.

| Week | Topic | What you'll learn |
|:-----|:------|:------------------|
| [Week 1](week1.qmd) | A fresh start | Why most published research is false: statistical significance, the base rate paradox, and Bayesian updating. |
| [Week 2](week2.qmd) | Describing data | Probability distributions, z-scores, correlation, and our first regression coefficient. Applied: what makes a house expensive? |
| [Week 3](week3.qmd) | Causes and DAGs | Drawing what causes what, what "cause" means in statistics, and the workflow from estimand to estimate. Worked example: does sex affect weight? |
| [Week 4](week4.qmd) | Confounding | The three building blocks of every DAG (fork, pipe, collider), the paradoxes each one creates, and how to decide what to control for. |
| [Week 5](week5.qmd) | Acting on evidence | Seven questions to ask of any finding, turning a decision into an estimand, and designing the experiment you wish you could run. |

# A Bayesian workflow

[A Bayesian Workflow](workflow.qmd) is a full worked example that pulls the course
together. It asks whether a university's admissions process discriminates by sex, and
goes through eight steps:

1. Define the estimand.
2. Draw the causal model (DAG).
3. Simulate the population.
4. Write the formal model.
5. Write the Stan code.
6. Test on simulated data.
7. Fit and validate the model.
8. Compute the estimand and test its robustness.

Along the way it shows Simpson's paradox: a large overall gap in admission rates that
disappears once we compare applicants to the same department.

# Homework

- [Week 1 homework](homework/week1.qmd): probability, base rates, and Bayesian updating.
- [Week 2 homework](homework/week2.qmd): distributions, z-scores, correlation, and regression.
- [Week 3 homework](homework/week3.qmd): DAGs, causes, and the workflow.
- [Week 4 homework](homework/week4.qmd): forks, pipes, colliders, and what to control for.
- [Week 5 homework](homework/week5.qmd): evaluating findings, estimands, and target trials.

# Student projects

Each student picks a question about development outcomes, draws a DAG, and fits a
Bayesian regression to the 2022 World Bank data. Nepal is highlighted throughout as the
reference case.

| Project | Question |
|:--------|:---------|
| [Archana](projects/archana.qmd) | Does access to drinking water services affect water stress? |
| [Ranju](projects/ranju.qmd) | Does corruption affect political stability? |
| [Sambit](projects/sambit.qmd) | Does internet use affect the share of young people not in education, employment or training (NEETs)? |
| [Sameer](projects/sameer.qmd) | Does the length of compulsory education affect vulnerable employment? |
| [Suyash](projects/suyash.qmd) | Does inflation affect GDP growth? |
| [Swasti](projects/swasti.qmd) | Does the share of youth NEETs affect net migration? |
| [Tsering](projects/tsering.qmd) | Does women's employment affect vulnerable employment? |
